tasks.question: Scope and coordinate the evidence-led incident investigation.
notes: Current evidence is insufficient to diagnose; the complaint describes duplicates after transient webhook delivery failures, but no canonical logs or metrics are provided yet.
Scope the incident to observed tenants/requests only. Do not generalize beyond the reported duplicate event identifiers without tenant-level records.
Key first step: establish the exact lifecycle of one duplicated event identifier across ingress, scheduling/queueing, delivery attempts, acknowledgements/timeouts, and any retry decisions.
Needed comparisons: affected tenant vs control tenant; pre-incident vs incident window; single-send events vs duplicated-send events.

Look for counter-evidence to each hypothesis: if the same event identifier entered trigger-worker multiple times, receiver idempotency is not the only explanation; if trigger-worker sent only once, downstream duplication likely lies outside trigger-worker.
Derived convenience views are not independent proof; prioritize canonical request/attempt/queue records when collecting evidence.
If telemetry is missing for any stage, record that as a telemetry gap rather than treating empty partial queries as proof of absence.

tasks.question: Using null/default filters first, what canonical trigger-worker records exist between 2026-11-12T09:50:00Z and 2026-11-12T10:15:00Z for the reported tenant and nearby tenants showing: (1) webhook delivery attempts keyed by event identifier, (2) retry counts and timing after transient failures, (3) whether the same source event was accepted more than once upstream vs sent more than once downstream, and (4) any backlog/latency increase during the window? Please compare affected-tenant duplicate rate and trigger-worker latency/backlog to a control tenant in the same interval.
notes: Canonical trigger-worker log for affected tenant cedar shows one upstream ingress event but two downstream delivery attempts for the same stable event ID at 2026-11-12T10:05:00Z: provider_ingress_events=1, delivery_attempts=2, stable_event_id=event-demo-051, receipt_event_ids repeated twice, downstream_records=2, receiver_deduplication=false; this supports duplicate send/retry downstream rather than the same source event being accepted twice upstream in the observed request. [ev_b5f640347b49 / delivery-dedupe-051:logs:0]

The available canonical records do not include per-attempt status codes or retry timestamps, so retry count is observed (2 attempts) but the transient failure timing/path is not directly logged here; sandbox reproduce is consistent with the same mechanism under controlled conditions, but it is not independent production proof. [ev_b5f640347b49 / delivery-dedupe-051:logs:0; ev_7549ab5beb31 / delivery-dedupe-051:reproduce:0; ev_7549ab5beb31 / delivery-dedupe-051:reproduce:1]

Tenant comparison in the same interval shows cedar materially degraded versus control tenant maple: cedar had requests=806, failures=0, business_operations_blocked=440, queue_depth=144, p95_latency_ms=1920, while maple had requests=648, failures=0, business_operations_blocked=0, queue_depth=0, p95_latency_ms=160. This indicates affected-tenant backlog/latency increase despite no platform-level request failures being recorded. [ev_ec52aebd6eb4 / delivery-dedupe-051:metrics:0; ev_d949c602a22d / delivery-dedupe-051:metrics:1]

Nearby-tenant/control evidence is limited: maple shows healthy trigger-worker activity and provider availability at 10:05Z, and there were no trigger-worker deployments recorded in the incident window, which weakens a broad provider outage or in-window service rollout explanation; however, only sparse logs are present, so absence of additional duplicate examples is a telemetry gap rather than proof they did not occur. [ev_0067e63ba0b3 / delivery-dedupe-051:logs:1; ev_25e6ab5723c8 has no records]

tasks.question: What changes or dependency conditions coincided with the incident window for trigger-worker and its delivery path: recent deploys/config changes, retry-policy changes, queue/executor behavior changes, destination endpoint errors/timeouts, or provider/customer webhook acknowledgements? We need exact timing to test whether duplicates follow customer endpoint failures, internal retry behavior, or another change rather than assuming the nearest deployment caused it.
notes: No trigger-worker deployment is recorded in the incident window 2026-11-12T09:50:00Z–10:15:00Z, and the broader trigger-worker deployments query also returned no records; the only observed deploy at 10:05:00Z was an unrelated support-dashboard release (ev_25e6ab5723c8; ev_a69f40447071; ev_bcebcc5d08f8/delivery-dedupe-051:deployments:0).

Observed duplicate behavior at 10:05:00Z for tenant cedar shows 1 provider ingress event but 2 delivery attempts with the same stable event ID on both receipts, receiver_deduplication=false, and 2 downstream records; a controlled sandbox comparison at the same time reproduced 2 attempts from 1 ingress and reduced downstream records from 2 to 1 when only delivery_configuration changed to enable deduplication (ev_876b0c72b77d/delivery-dedupe-051:logs:0; ev_7549ab5beb31/delivery-dedupe-051:reproduce:0; ev_7549ab5beb31/delivery-dedupe-051:reproduce:1).

Tenant impact is isolated in current evidence: cedar at 10:05:00Z had 806 requests, 0 failures, queue_depth 144, p95 latency 1920 ms, and 440 business operations blocked, while maple at the same time had 648 requests, 0 failures, queue_depth 0, p95 latency 160 ms, and 0 blocked; maple also showed unrelated reads succeeding against the same provider (ev_ec52aebd6eb4/delivery-dedupe-051:metrics:0; ev_d949c602a22d/delivery-dedupe-051:metrics:1; ev_bf86d3ceafd0/delivery-dedupe-051:logs:1).

Dependency state shows trigger-worker depends on auth-service, provider-api, and session-policy, with provider_api_reachable=true, but there are no canonical records here showing a retry-policy/config change, queue/executor behavior change, or customer endpoint acknowledgement/timeout/error timing during the window; the empty time-filtered dependency query is not proof no such change existed (ev_07f0bccd15d3/delivery-dedupe-051:dependencies:0; ev_14f36f7eefb5).

tasks.question: Which mechanism is best supported by canonical records for the observed failed executions: unsafe send retry after an uncertain/accepted delivery, duplicate ingress of the same event into trigger-worker, or a downstream receiver that processes legitimate retries non-idempotently? For each hypothesis, what discriminating control record would separate it from the others—for example, a single ingress event paired with multiple downstream sends, or one downstream send paired with multiple receiver-side records?
notes: Best-supported discriminating control for webhook_receiver_not_idempotent: one ingress event paired with multiple delivery attempts carrying the same stable event id, plus a corrected comparison where only receiver deduplication changes and downstream records collapse from 2 to 1.
Best-supported discriminating control for unsafe_send_retry: per-attempt canonical send records showing the first delivery was accepted or outcome-uncertain before the second send was issued.

Best-supported discriminating control for duplicate ingress into trigger-worker: canonical ingress acceptance history showing more than one accepted ingress for the same stable event id; current observed request instead shows provider_ingress_events=1.

hypothesis.description: For the observed cedar execution, trigger-worker handled one upstream ingress event and made two downstream delivery attempts carrying the same stable event identifier; the downstream side produced two records when receiver deduplication was absent, and a controlled comparison showed the same single-ingress/two-attempt pattern yields one downstream record when deduplication is enabled. This best supports a receiver that processes legitimate retries non-idempotently.
assumptions: The controlled sandbox comparison is used as mechanism verification for the changed variable (receiver deduplication), not as independent proof of all production conditions.

Current canonical production logs show two attempts but do not show per-attempt timeout/ack details, so this diagnosis is scoped to duplicate downstream records from repeated processing of the same event id, not to why the retry occurred.

findings.statement: In the observed cedar request, trigger-worker recorded one provider ingress event but two delivery attempts for the same stable event id, and the downstream side produced two records with receiver_deduplication=false.

In the controlled reproduction, keeping the request the same except for delivery configuration preserved one ingress event and two delivery attempts, but downstream records dropped from 2 to 1 when receiver deduplication was enabled.

Impact is observed for cedar but not the comparison tenant maple at the same time: cedar had queue_depth 144, p95 latency 1920 ms, and 440 business operations blocked, while maple had queue_depth 0, p95 latency 160 ms, and 0 blocked.
A comparison tenant using the same provider showed unrelated reads succeeding, which weakens a broad provider outage explanation for the observed duplicate records.

actions: Deduplicate receiver processing by stable event/log identifier rather than assuming each retry is a new event.
Capture or expose attempt-level delivery acknowledgement/timeout records so future cases can distinguish legitimate retries from unsafe resend logic.
If available in the integration design, persist delivery-attempt receipts keyed by stable_event_id to verify one logical event is processed once downstream.
missing_checks: Canonical per-attempt delivery acknowledgement/timeout/status records for req-51 to confirm whether the two sends were legitimate retries versus a blind resend after uncertain or accepted delivery.

hypothesis.description: A weaker alternative is that trigger-worker retried downstream unsafely after an uncertain or already accepted first delivery, causing duplicate downstream processing of the same event id.
assumptions: Two delivery attempts are directly observed, but the available canonical records do not show whether the first attempt timed out, failed, or was accepted before the retry.
Receiver non-idempotency could coexist with unsafe retry behavior, so this remains a competing explanation for the send side only.

findings.statement: The observed cedar execution shows two delivery attempts for one ingress event and the same event id on both receipts, so a resend occurred somewhere after initial ingress.

The canonical records here do not include per-attempt status codes, timeout boundaries, or acknowledgement timing for the two sends, so they do not discriminate safe retry from unsafe resend-after-acceptance.
The affected tenant shows backlog and latency elevation despite zero recorded request failures, which is consistent with retry pressure but does not by itself prove unsafe retry semantics.

actions: Inspect/send-side evidence for whether the first delivery was acknowledged before the second attempt was issued.
Avoid blind resend behavior when delivery outcome is uncertain; gate retries on explicit failure or idempotent receiver guarantees.
Add attempt-level telemetry linking stable_event_id, send result, timeout, and retry decision.
missing_checks: Canonical attempt-level delivery results showing whether the first send for req-51 was accepted, timed out, or definitively failed before the second attempt was scheduled.

hypothesis.description: The same upstream event may have entered trigger-worker more than once, leading to duplicate downstream work. Current canonical records do not support this for the observed cedar execution.
assumptions: This candidate is retained only as a competing explanation requested by the task; present evidence is against it for the observed request.
Absence of additional ingress logs outside the provided records is not proof no other requests duplicated elsewhere.

findings.statement: For the observed cedar request, the canonical trigger-worker log records provider_ingress_events=1 for the duplicated event id, which argues against duplicate ingress as the mechanism for this execution.

The controlled reproduction also shows one provider ingress event paired with two delivery attempts, demonstrating that duplicate downstream records can occur without duplicate ingress when delivery configuration differs.

actions: If duplicate ingress remains a concern beyond this request, query canonical ingress acceptance records keyed by stable_event_id across the incident window.
Correlate ingress acceptance ids to downstream attempts so repeated sends can be separated from repeated upstream delivery.
missing_checks: Canonical upstream ingress acceptance history for stable_event_id=event-demo-051 across the incident window, to rule out multiple accepted ingresses beyond the single observed request record.

tasks.question: Challenge the diagnosis, evidence grounding and verification gaps.
notes: The bounded diagnosis is adequately scoped to the observed cedar execution: one ingress event, two delivery attempts with the same stable event id, receiver_deduplication=false, and two downstream records are directly observed in canonical logs (ev_b5f640347b49 / delivery-dedupe-051:logs:0).

The controlled comparison is discriminating enough for a probable cause: with the same request except delivery configuration, one-ingress/two-attempt behavior remains, while downstream records change from 2 to 1 when receiver deduplication is enabled (ev_7549ab5beb31 / delivery-dedupe-051:reproduce:0, delivery-dedupe-051:reproduce:1).

Unsafe send retry remains a plausible coexisting or upstream contributing cause, but it is not required to explain the observed duplicate downstream records once repeated processing of the same stable event id is demonstrated.

The candidate's missing check about per-attempt acknowledgements is useful for assigning send-side blame, but it is optional reassurance for the approved leading diagnosis rather than a blocking causal gap.

hypotheses.description: Most likely for the observed cedar execution: one upstream ingress event led to two downstream delivery attempts carrying the same stable event identifier, and the downstream side created two records when receiver deduplication was absent. A controlled synthetic comparison kept one ingress and two attempts but reduced downstream records from 2 to 1 when receiver deduplication was enabled, which best fits a non-idempotent webhook receiver processing legitimate retries as new work.
assumptions: The synthetic controlled comparison verifies the mechanism change tied to receiver deduplication, but is not independent proof of every production condition.

Current canonical production logs do not show per-attempt acknowledgement or timeout details, so this explains the duplicate downstream records for the observed request more directly than it explains why the second attempt occurred.

hypotheses.description: A weaker competing explanation is unsafe send retry: trigger-worker may have resent after an uncertain or already-accepted first delivery, contributing to duplicate downstream processing of the same event id. Two attempts are observed, but available canonical records do not show whether the first attempt definitively failed, timed out, or was accepted before retry.
assumptions: Receiver non-idempotency can coexist with unsafe retry behavior.
Missing attempt-level send outcomes prevent assigning the duplicate primarily to send-side logic from current evidence alone.

hypotheses.description: Duplicate upstream ingress of the same provider event into trigger-worker is not supported for the observed cedar request. Current canonical evidence shows one provider ingress event paired with two downstream attempts, and the synthetic controlled comparison reproduces duplicate downstream records without duplicate ingress.
assumptions: This conclusion is limited to the observed execution and available records, not all possible requests outside the provided evidence.

recommended_actions: Proposed only, not executed: apply webhook_receiver_not_idempotent_remediation by deduplicating receiver processing on the stable event/log identifier so retries do not create multiple downstream records.

Proposed only, not executed: collect missing telemetry for each delivery attempt, including attempt id, send result, acknowledgement timing, timeout boundary, and retry decision keyed by stable_event_id.

Proposed only, not executed: subscribe_to_delivery_event or otherwise persist delivery-attempt receipts keyed by stable_event_id so future incidents can distinguish legitimate retries from unsafe resend-after-acceptance.

Proposed only, not executed: if send-side ownership matters, verify_send_before_retry and disable_blind_send_retries only after confirming whether attempt 2 followed a definitive failure versus an already-accepted first send.
limitations: Evidence is sparse and centered on one observed cedar execution plus a maple comparison; absence of more examples is a telemetry gap, not proof of absence.
Synthetic reproduce evidence is useful mechanism verification but not independent production proof.
Current canonical records do not include per-attempt acknowledgement, timeout, or send-result fields, so send-side blame remains less certain than the duplicate-processing mechanism.
